perspective:
Mason’s available information is limited to his own work context, observations, statements he heard, and his own thoughts/actions:

- He is an accountant at a small community center. Martha Moua is his colleague there, a personal care aide; they have a professional but not close relationship.
- While reviewing financial reports, he saw discrepancies, especially unusually high healthcare expenses that did not match usual spending patterns.
- Based on this, he became suspicious and anxious, suspecting Martha might be mismanaging funds.
- He asked Martha to discuss the report, said the numbers did not add up, and pointed to the healthcare expenses.
- He heard Martha say there might have been a misentry, and that she would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing/clarifying with Martha, he understood the discrepancies were a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. He felt relieved but embarrassed about his initial suspicion.
- He thanked Martha for quickly clarifying, apologized for suspecting her, and said he should have asked her first.
- He heard Martha say errors happen, she understood he was being thorough, and they should double-check entries next time.
- He then believed Martha was competent. He believed recurring clerical errors pointed to inadequate financial management systems, and he felt frustrated with the system but empathetic toward Martha.
- He told Martha the issue was not her management but the current system. He proposed a new, more robust financial system, said he would draft a proposal, and asked for her input.
- He heard Martha agree, say it was a great idea, and offer to help address the gaps.
- He drafted the proposal. He hoped it would benefit operations but was uncertain whether management would approve or implement it.
- He told Martha he had finished the draft and was unsure how management would receive it.
- He heard Martha say it was a solid proposal, that he should present it confidently, and that its benefits were clear.
- He planned a detailed presentation and asked Martha to help gather data to strengthen their case. He heard her agree.
- After presenting the proposal to management, he felt satisfied with his effort but physically and mentally exhausted. He believed he had done everything possible and that the decision was now up to management.
- He told Martha the presentation went well and it was up to management. He heard Martha praise his work and suggest taking time off.
- He thanked Martha for her support, said he would take a few days off to recharge and reflect, and hoped they would return to good news.
- He heard Martha tell him to enjoy his break and let her know if he needed anything while away.
- He does not yet know management’s decision about the proposal.
